title: What is induction training?
description: Induction training prepares new or transferred workers, contractors and visitors to work safely from day one. What the law requires and what to cover.
shortAnswer: Induction training is the structured introduction a worker, contractor or visitor receives before or on starting work in a new organization, site or role, covering the hazards, rules, procedures, emergency arrangements and responsibilities they need to work safely and correctly from day one. Many safety laws require it, for example the EU OSH Framework Directive's training on recruitment, Japan's education on hiring, and Australia's general construction induction for construction workers.
keyTakeaways: Induction training is required at the start of work in many jurisdictions, and often again on transfer, change of job or new equipment.
There are usually three layers: organization wide induction, site induction and role or task induction.
Contractors and visitors need induction proportionate to their exposure; the EU Framework Directive requires employers to ensure outside workers have received appropriate instructions.
Industry wide inductions, such as Australia's general construction induction card, do not replace site specific induction.
Effective inductions check understanding of critical content rather than relying on attendance or a signature.

sections.heading: Is induction training a legal requirement?

blocks.text: In many jurisdictions, yes: safety laws require employers to train workers when they start, even where the law does not use the word induction. Three examples show the pattern.

items: **European Union.** [Council Directive 89/391/EEC, Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391), requires employers to ensure each worker receives adequate safety and health training specific to their workstation or job "on recruitment", on transfer or change of job, and on the introduction of new work equipment or technology. Article 12(2) requires employers to ensure that workers from outside undertakings working in their establishment "have in fact received appropriate instructions" on the health and safety risks of their activities.

**Japan.** [Article 59(1) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act](https://www.japaneselawtranslation.go.jp/en/laws/view/3440) provides that, having begun to employ a new worker, the employer must educate that worker in safety or health as it relates to the operations the worker will do, and article 59(2) applies the same duty when the substance of the work changes. The Japanese Law Translation database notes that only the original Japanese text has legal effect ([e-Gov text](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057)).

**Australia.** The [model WHS Regulations](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-12/model-whs-regulations-5_december_2025.pdf) require a person conducting a business or undertaking to ensure general construction induction training is provided to a worker who is to carry out construction work, and not to direct or allow construction work unless the worker has completed it (regulations 316 and 317). Training completed more than two years earlier must be repeated if the worker has not done construction work in the preceding two years.

blocks.text: In the United States, many OSHA standards require training "at the time of initial assignment", for example the bloodborne pathogens standard, [29 CFR 1910.1030(g)(2)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-Z/section-1910.1030), which builds a topic specific induction duty into each standard.

Induction should cover what a person must know before they can work without causing harm, in three layers. Content beyond that belongs in later onboarding or role training, so the induction stays focused.

blocks.caption: Induction layers: content, audience and evidence (original)
head: Layer
Typical content
Who receives it
Evidence of understanding
rows: Safety policy, reporting hazards and incidents, code of conduct, key compliance obligations, how to raise concerns
Short knowledge check on reporting routes and critical rules
Site hazards, traffic and exclusion zones, emergency procedures and assembly points, first aid, permits, PPE
Workers, contractors and, in a shorter form, visitors
Site walk with a supervisor, questions on emergency actions
Procedures, equipment, task hazards and controls, who to ask, limits of authority, required competencies
Each worker for their role; again on transfer or change of job
Observed task performance or [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) before unsupervised work

blocks.text: Mapping induction content to the obligations behind it, and to roles, is described in [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles).

sections.heading: Do contractors and visitors need induction training?

blocks.text: Yes, in proportion to their exposure to the site's hazards. Contractors doing work usually need the site and task layers; visitors who are escorted and do no work usually need a short briefing on hazards and emergency procedures. The EU Framework Directive's Article 12(2) puts the onus on the host employer to ensure outside workers have actually received appropriate instructions.

A portable credential, such as an Australian general construction induction card or an entry in a [skills passport](/glossary/skills-passport), shows that general training was completed. It does not cover the specific hazards and procedures of your site, so site induction is still needed.

sections.heading: How is induction training different from onboarding or refresher training?

blocks.text: Induction is the first, safety and compliance critical part of onboarding; onboarding is the broader process of integrating a new person into the organization over weeks or months. [Refresher training](/glossary/refresher-training) comes later and maintains what induction and role training established. Some rules require induction to be repeated, for example after a break from construction work under the model WHS Regulations, which blurs the line, so define each term in your [training policy](/guides/how-to-write-a-training-policy).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures induction content from the obligations, hazards and procedures that apply to each layer and role, with assessment points on the critical items. When a site procedure or rule changes, the affected induction content and the people already inducted are identified for update.

faqs.q: How long should induction training take?
faqs.a: Long enough to cover what the person needs to work safely from day one, and no longer. Some rules set minimum content or hours for specific inductions, but most leave length to the employer. Splitting non critical content into later onboarding keeps the induction focused.

faqs.q: Can induction training be done online?
faqs.a: Organization level content often can. Site and task content usually needs practical elements, such as a walk through of emergency routes or a demonstration of a task, that online modules alone cannot provide. Check whether any rule specifies face to face delivery.

faqs.q: Is a signed induction form enough evidence?
faqs.a: A signature shows attendance, not understanding. Stronger evidence combines the record of what was covered with a check of understanding on critical items, such as emergency actions and stop work authority, and an observed task before unsupervised work.

faqs.q: When should induction training be repeated?
faqs.a: When a worker changes job or site, when significant new equipment, technology or procedures are introduced, after a long absence, and whenever a specific rule requires it. The EU Framework Directive lists transfer, change of job and new equipment or technology as triggers.
